shots.text: An AI agent wrote this pull request. Ninety two files. Your name goes on the approval.
Countersign says eight lines are yours. The rule: skip a line only when a run covers it. Sign by name for everything else.
On pull request five, the brief asks Aino for about two minutes. Read eight of two hundred and ten lines.
The other two hundred and two are one two line edit, in ninety files. A script checked every file. A passing test run regenerated them.

calls.text: Second model on the skip: nothing raised

shots.text: The reviewer is tested too. Five bugs were planted by another model family. It caught four. A second model read the skipped lines, and raised nothing.

calls.text: The PR's tests pass without the change

shots.text: Pull request two is heavier. Here the AI found a real gap, and proved it with a test that fails.

calls.text: The AI will not decide this

shots.text: Here it refuses to decide. You get the options, and no recommendation.

calls.text: Mark read waits for the reading floor

shots.text: And these lines are yours. Mark read stays locked until you have had time to read them.
Aino holds to countersign. Her statement lists what the AI checked, what she read, what nobody checked, and the risk she accepts.

calls.text: After a signature: green, under a name

shots.text: On GitHub, the check is required. GitHub blocks the merge until a person signs. Then the check turns green, under their name.
Trust is measured, and kept apart. What we measured here. A backtest on merged history. And seeded history, never mixed in.
Trust is earned per code area. One escape drops it.
When do we distrust our own output? No requirement. Nothing ran. The reviewer missed a planted bug. An area on probation. A spot check. Then every line is read.
Who owns the decision? The person who signs.
How does it scale? Reading follows risk, not diff size. Ninety two files. Eight lines.
Countersign. AI reviews. A named human countersigns.
